one_liner: CPU (and CUDA) nonuniform FFT library, types 1-3 in 1-3 dimensions, several times faster than NFFT3 and CMCL NUFFT.
what_it_does: Computes nonuniform FFTs to a user-chosen relative tolerance: type 1 (nonuniform points to uniform Fourier modes, NFFT3's 'adjoint'), type 2 (modes to nonuniform points) and type 3 (nonuniform to nonuniform), in 1, 2 or 3 dimensions, single or double precision. The C/C++ API has simple calls (finufft2d1 etc.), vectorized 'many' calls for stacks of transforms sharing points, and a guru plan interface (makeplan, setpts, execute, execute_adjoint, destroy); MATLAB/Octave, Python (pip finufft / cufinufft), Fortran and Julia wrappers exist. It is not a drop-in for NFFT3: arrays are column-major, the exponent has no 2*pi factor (points live on a 2*pi-periodic box), and the tolerance must be passed explicitly; docs/nfft_migr.rst shows the conversion.
how_it_is_fast: Standard spread / FFT / deconvolve NUFFT, but with a cheap compactly supported kernel evaluated on the fly by Horner piecewise polynomials and SIMD (xsimd) instead of precomputed kernel tables, so no point-dependent precomputation or large RAM is needed. Points are bin-sorted for cache locality and type-1 spreading is split into load-balanced subproblems across OpenMP threads; the inner FFT is FFTW (default) or DUCC0, which exploits the block sparsity of the upsampled 2D/3D grids. The 2019 paper introduced the 'exponential of semicircle' kernel; since v2.5.0 the default is a PSWF (prolate) kernel, and upsampfac=0 picks the oversampling factor (for example 2 or 1.25) from a density-aware cost model.
when_to_use: MRI, cryo-EM, radio-astronomy imaging, spectral analysis of unevenly sampled data or PDE solvers that need sums of exponentials at nonuniform points, where a direct O(NM) sum or NFFT3 is too slow.
2-D and 3-D problems with up to millions of points at tolerances from about 1e-2 to 1e-12 in double precision (about 1e-5 in single), on multicore CPUs.

Repeated transforms with the same points: the guru or 'many' interface reuses the bin-sort and FFT plan, which the troubleshooting page says can be 10-100x faster than repeated simple calls on small problems.
NVIDIA GPU workloads through cuFINUFFT in the same repository, whose legacy README claims up to 10x over CPU FINUFFT and up to 100x over other established GPU NUFFT codes.
Projects that need one library with C, C++, Python, MATLAB/Octave, Fortran and Julia front ends under Apache-2.0.
when_not_to_use: Data on a regular grid: a plain FFT is faster and exact, and type 1 and type 2 are adjoints, not inverses, so you cannot undo one with the other; NFFT3 has inverse NUFFTs, sphere and rotation-group transforms that FINUFFT lacks.

Very many tiny transforms through the simple interface, or very high thread counts: FFTW wisdom lookup costs about 0.1 ms per thread, and open issue #869 reports a 3-D grid running 50-80x slower at 96 threads than at 64 or fewer on a dual EPYC 9474F.

Tolerances near machine precision or large 1-D N in single precision: errors cannot beat roughly N_max times machine epsilon, and requests the library judges unreachable return error 26 unless opts.allow_eps_too_small is set.
Every regime against DUCC's own NUFFT: the project's docs say DUCC 'in some regimes is faster than ours', and NonuniformFFTs.jl is close on CPU and faster for real-valued data.
Bitwise reproducibility across thread counts: results vary at rounding level, by up to about 1e-11 relative in double with upsampfac=1.25 at tol 1e-7 to 1e-9.

integration.dependencies: FFTW3 >= 3.3.6 single and double (default) or DUCC0 (fetched and bundled by CMake), xsimd and POET header-only (fetched), OpenMP (optional, ON by default); CUDA 11.8+ for cuFINUFFT
integration.min_toolchain: C++17, CMake 3.25; GCC 9+ recommended on x86-64 (GCC 8.5 can fail in xsimd with AVX-512); MSVC works on Windows
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon), Windows (MSVC or MinGW; Windows CI builds DUCC0 only), PowerPC64/64le cross-builds; NVIDIA GPUs via cuFINUFFT; builds default to -march=native
integration.thread_safety: Documented: safe with DUCC0; with FFTW, safe as long as no other thread creates or destroys FFTW plans outside FINUFFT (call fftw_make_planner_thread_safe() or pass opts.fftw_lock_fun/fftw_unlock_fun); set opts.nthreads=1 when calling from inside your own parallel region.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the NFFT3 migration guide maps type-1 calls one to one, but coordinates must be rescaled by 2*pi and x/y swapped (row-major vs column-major), and NFFT3's inverse and special-geometry transforms have no equivalent

gotchas: setpts keeps pointers to your nonuniform point arrays rather than copying them, so they must stay unchanged until the last execute that uses them.
The default FFTW plan mode is FFTW_ESTIMATE; FFTW_MEASURE gives faster repeated transforms but can spend many seconds planning on the first call.

v2.5.0 switched the default kernel to PSWF, which changes results at the tolerance level, and its kernel setup was not thread safe when plans are created concurrently (fixed in v2.5.1, #835/#838); open issue #839 reports a rare heap-corruption abort in that code path during parallel plan creation, not yet diagnosed.

Unreleased master (v2.6.0-dev) fixes a Windows fine-grid size wraparound that silently ran transforms on a tiny grid, a clang -fassociative-math build that folded points wrongly and segfaulted, and an icpx bin-sort miscompile; build from master or a later release if you hit these configurations.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It is the general-purpose NUFFT among the catalogued FFT entries: pick it over TRON when you need all three transform types, CPU support and arbitrary sampling rather than a GPU MRI gridding pipeline compared against gpuNUFFT. Uniform-grid FFT entries (Admiral, PocketFFT, VkFFT) and FFTW++'s padded convolutions solve a different problem and are only relevant as its inner FFT or for regularly sampled data.
verified_claims_summary: docs/nfft_migr.rst times a 2-D type-1 transform of 500,000 random points to 300 x 200 modes at tol 1e-13, single thread on an AMD 5700U laptop: NFFT3 3.5.4alpha 0.589 s versus FINUFFT 0.0787 s (7.5x), with the same output to all printed digits (compiler and flags not stated; the timing uses clock()). The peer-reviewed 2019 SIAM J. Sci. Comput. paper, seen only through a WebSearch summary because arxiv.org is blocked here, reports NFFT 3.3.2 as 3-5x slower without precomputation and 2-4x slower with it, FINUFFT at least 2x faster than every other code tested on random points except MIRT at 1-digit accuracy, and CMCL NUFFT up to 50x slower even on one thread (docs/related.rst).
